title: CA Sri Lanka submits sweeping proposals for Budget 2027 | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 15 September 2026 06:08
-     - 10

CA Sri Lanka President Tishan Subasinghe (right) in conversation with Finance Ministry Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma following the submission of proposals to Budget 2027

Advocates compliance-led revenue growth, digital transformation, taxpayer fairness and more competitive business environment

Proposes revising Advance Personal Income Tax threshold to Rs. 200,000 per month, providing relief to middle-income earners

Estimates measure would result in approximate revenue contraction of 

Rs. 26 b against 2026 baseline and Rs. 79 b compared with 2025 actual revenue

Moots next phase of enhancing tax compliance should focus on connecting taxpayer registration with economic activity, ownership, financial transactions and cross-agency information

Recommends establishing integrated data ecosystem through National Taxpayer Information Network and Universal Business Identification Number, connecting information from Customs, VAT transactions, corporate ownership, financial accounts, property records and other relevant datasets

Urges to move progressively from volume-based enforcement towards formal Compliance Risk Management framework, classifying taxpayers according to low, medium and high risk

To support formalisation and sustainable growth, especially SMEs, proposes tiered corporate income tax structure based on annual turnover

The Institute of Chartered Accountants of Sri Lanka (CA Sri Lanka) yesterday said it has submitted its comprehensive proposals for the National Budget 2027 to Finance Ministry Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma.

The proposals were submitted by CA Sri Lanka President Tishan Subasinghe, accompanied by Members of the Council, Faculty of Taxation Alternate Chairman Prasad Dasanayaka, and CEO Lakmali Priyangika.

The 16-page proposals, developed through extensive consultations with members and deliberations at the Institute’s 5th Annual Economic and Tax Symposium, present a comprehensive roadmap for strengthening Sri Lanka’s fiscal position through improved compliance, digitalisation, formalization, and taxpayer confidence, while supporting investment and sustainable economic growth.

Presenting the proposals, Subasinghe emphasised that Sri Lanka’s next phase of fiscal reform must move beyond repeated increases in statutory tax rates.

“Sri Lanka has made commendable progress in restoring macroeconomic stability and rebuilding fiscal credibility, but we cannot sustain this momentum through excessive reliance on tax rate hikes alone,” Subasinghe said.

“Our focus must now shift towards better capturing the economic activity already taking place across the country and bringing more of it into the formal tax system. We need to broaden and strengthen the tax base through improved compliance, better use of information and more predictable tax administration. The Institute believes that by prioritising digitalisation, formalization, and taxpayer confidence, we can mobilise revenue fairly and efficiently while fostering an environment conducive to investment and sustainable growth,” he said.

The proposals are anchored on three complementary objectives: mobilising additional revenue without excessive reliance on higher statutory tax rates; modernising tax administration and improving voluntary compliance; and strengthening the investment, business, and institutional environment required for sustainable growth.

CA Sri Lanka highlights the fragility of Sri Lanka’s current revenue structure, which remains heavily dependent on indirect taxation. In 2025, indirect taxes accounted for approximately 11.9% of GDP, compared with only 3.5% from income taxes.

The Institute notes that this imbalance places a disproportionate burden on consumers and can contribute to informal economic activity. It therefore proposes a clear hierarchy for revenue mobilisation, with statutory rate increases considered only after other avenues have been exhausted.

The proposed hierarchy is:

*Improve compliance with existing taxes;

*Identify economic activity that currently remains untaxed;

*Reduce revenue leakages;

*Broaden the tax base through digitalisation and better information;

*Review and rationalise tax exemptions; and

*Only then consider broad statutory rate increases.

This approach, the Institute believes, would enable Sri Lanka to strengthen revenue mobilisation while minimising unnecessary pressure on compliant taxpayers and businesses.

Connecting registration to economic activity

The proposals highlight that while Sri Lanka’s registered taxpayer population increased from 1,239,541 in 2024 to 1,470,011 in 2025, an increase of approximately 18.6%, registration alone does not guarantee effective compliance or revenue mobilisation.

“The next phase should focus on connecting taxpayer registration with economic activity, ownership, financial transactions and cross-agency information,” the proposals state.

CA Sri Lanka therefore recommends establishing an integrated data ecosystem through the National Taxpayer Information Network (NTIN) and Universal Business Identification Number (UBIN), connecting information from Customs, VAT transactions, corporate ownership, financial accounts, property records, and other relevant datasets.

The Institute proposes that the UBIN, NTIN and electronic invoicing should be developed as part of the wider World Bank-supported digital transformation agenda, ultimately contributing towards a single digital economic identity that can improve both revenue administration and the delivery of Government services.

Harnessing data and Artificial Intelligence for compliance

The proposals call for Sri Lanka to move progressively from volume-based enforcement towards a formal Compliance Risk Management framework, classifying taxpayers according to low, medium, and high risk.

As part of this transition, CA Sri Lanka proposes an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted Tax Compliance Risk Engine to identify potential high-risk cases involving shell companies, unexplained wealth, circular transactions, and Value Added Tax (VAT) fraud. The system would function as a selection and risk-identification tool rather than a final determinant of tax liability, ensuring that technology supports professional assessment and due process rather than replacing them.

The Institute also recommends strengthening the existing High-Wealth Individual (HWI) Compliance Program through a formal wealth-to-income risk model.

To address gaps between actual economic capacity and reported income, the proposals recommend enhanced monitoring of financial assets, cryptocurrencies, and insurance investments through annual information returns.

CA Sri Lanka further proposes a VAT Intelligence Program, initially as a pilot initiative, using objective indicators such as electricity consumption, bank deposits, and point-of-sale (POS) data to identify potential compliance risks in high-risk, cash-intensive sectors, including gold and auto-parts businesses.

Modernising VAT and Customs administration

The Institute recommends the phased introduction of mandatory electronic invoicing, beginning with large VAT taxpayers and high-risk sectors before progressively expanding across the wider business community.

It also proposes automated Customs–Import Data Reconciliation, comparing Customs values and landed costs against inventory, sales, VAT, and income tax returns to identify potential revenue leakages, particularly in import-dependent sectors.

The proposals also identify the need to address unregulated economic activity in specific sectors. In the broadcasting sector, CA Sri Lanka recommends action to address an estimated 300,000 illegal Direct-to-Home (DTH) connections, which are estimated to generate approximately Rs. 3.6 billion in unregulated revenue, with potential tax recovery estimated at around Rs. 1.5 billion.

Tax relief while protecting revenue

CA Sri Lanka proposes revising the Advance Personal Income Tax (APIT) threshold to Rs. 200,000 per month, providing relief to middle-income earners.

The Institute estimates that the measure would result in an approximate revenue contraction of Rs. 26.01 billion against the 2026 baseline and Rs. 79.08 billion compared with 2025 actual revenue.

While recognising the fiscal impact, CA Sri Lanka believes the measure could stimulate economic activity and improve disposable income amid continuing inflationary pressures. The proposals therefore emphasise that the fiscal cost should be considered alongside the potential economic benefits of increased consumption and formal economic activity.

A proportionate tax framework for SMEs

To support formalisation and sustainable growth, CA Sri Lanka proposes a tiered corporate income tax structure based on annual turnover.

The proposed framework would recognise:

*Micro enterprises: annual turnover up to Rs. 20 million;

*Small enterprises: annual turnover up to Rs. 350 million;

*Medium enterprises: annual turnover up to Rs. 1 billion; and

*Large enterprises: annual turnover exceeding Rs. 1 billion.

The structure would be supported by a proportionality principle in tax compliance, recognising that smaller businesses should not face the same administrative burden as larger corporations.

Micro businesses should be able to maintain simplified records, while small and medium-sized businesses (SMEs) could progressively adopt standardised digital templates. The objective is to encourage businesses to formalise and grow without excessive compliance requirements inadvertently pushing smaller enterprises into informality.

The Institute also recommends that the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) encourage financial institutions to rely, where appropriate, on audited financial statements and tax returns when assessing credit applications, thereby reducing the need for SMEs to incur additional costs to satisfy lending requirements.

CA Sri Lanka further calls for the urgent expedition of Development Banks’ concessionary lending facilities for SMEs, with access linked to the submission of audited accounts. This would provide much-needed support to businesses facing current cash-flow constraints while simultaneously encouraging stronger financial reporting practices.

Strengthening capital gains and tourism taxation

The CA Sri Lanka proposals also call for stronger and more transparent capital gains assessments, including a framework under which valuations prepared by accredited independent professionals are formally considered by the Inland Revenue Department (IRD).

For tourism, CA Sri Lanka recommends a dedicated Digital Tourism Booking Framework to address tax-base erosion associated with non-resident digital platforms facilitating accommodation bookings in Sri Lanka.

The framework would seek to capture offshore deductions and related economic value, including booking commissions, franchise royalties, and global marketing fees paid to non-resident platforms, ensuring that Sri Lanka’s tax base appropriately reflects the economic activity generated within the country.

Strengthening taxpayer rights and predictability

CA Sri Lanka also proposes a statutory Right to Self-Correction, allowing taxpayers to correct genuine errors while distinguishing taxpayer-initiated corrections from pre-assessment correction opportunities.

The Institute also recommends establishing an Independent Taxpayer Ombudsman to address complaints relating to administrative treatment, unreasonable delays, communication failures, and systemic service issues.

In addition, the proposals call for a Tax Administration Service Charter establishing clear standards for fairness, timeliness, communication, and adequate advance notice of compliance requirements. This would help prevent situations where taxpayers face retrospective compliance difficulties following sudden changes in requirements, such as changes to VAT invoice procedures.

CA Sri Lanka also proposes amending the law to allow the Commissioner-General of Inland Revenue to waive or reduce disproportionate interest on just and equitable grounds, where appropriate.

A further holdover provision is proposed to suspend tax collection during the appeal process in qualifying cases. This would help prevent undue financial pressure on taxpayers and reduce the risk of coercive settlements while legitimate disputes are being determined.

Building a modern Inland Revenue Department

The Institute stresses that reform of the IRD must go beyond simply filling existing vacancies.

While CA Sri Lanka calls for the urgent filling of 223 senior-level vacancies, it also recommends lateral recruitment for specialised technical positions, including data scientists and other digital and analytical professionals.

Continuous professional development should form an integral part of this transformation, including training partnerships with professional bodies such as CA Sri Lanka in specialised areas such as international taxation and transfer pricing.

The proposals also recommend establishing a permanent Tax Policy and Revenue Analytics Unit within the Finance Ministry to undertake tax-gap analysis, tax expenditure evaluation, and revenue forecasting.

To strengthen transparency and accountability, the Institute proposes the publication of information relating to tax expenditure, tax arrears, and key compliance indicators.

International taxation and emerging revenue issues

CA Sri Lanka recommends a formal assessment of Sri Lanka’s exposure to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s (OECD) 15% global minimum effective tax rate under Pillar Two, together with consideration of a Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax (QDMTT) to protect the domestic tax base.

The Institute also recommends restoring the real tax share on cigarettes towards the World Health Organisation (WHO) benchmark of 75%, with estimated annual revenue recovery of Rs. 17.3 billion, subject to Treasury validation.

However, CA Sri Lanka stresses the importance of evidence-based policymaking. Estimates relating to cigarette excise reform should be validated against possible illicit-market effects, while potential QDMTT revenue cannot be responsibly estimated without multinational enterprise-level GloBE income data.

Similarly, revenue estimates associated with NTIN, HWI compliance, and Customs reconciliation should be supported by formal tax-gap studies.

A reform agenda built on evidence and trust

CA Sri Lanka emphasises that all major tax and revenue proposals should undergo a formal Revenue Impact Assessment before being considered for inclusion in the National Budget.

The Institute urges the Government to give immediate priority to integrated tax data, HWI compliance, Customs–IRD reconciliation, and Pillar Two implementation, while progressively building the digital and institutional infrastructure required for a modern revenue administration.

Subasinghe said: “Fiscal consolidation cannot be sustained through repeated increases in statutory tax rates alone. Our proposals offer a balanced approach that strengthens compliance, leverages digitalisation, protects taxpayer rights, and creates a more predictable and fair tax environment that can support sustainable economic growth and improved public confidence.”

“As the national body of accountants, we stand ready to work with the Government in implementing these reforms and contributing to Sri Lanka’s journey from resilience to revival,” Subasinghe added.

title: Ex-envoy Mahinda urges speedier finalisation of new tariff deal with US by Sri Lanka | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 15 September 2026 06:06
-     - 8

Sri Lanka's former Ambassador to the US Mahinda Samarasinghe -Pic by Lasantha Kumara

Former Ambassador Mahinda Samarasinghe yesterday called for an early conclusion of the bilateral agreement with the United States on the new tariff regime so as to safeguard the former’s interests in terms of crucial exports and future investments.

Delivering the keynote at the Sri Lanka Institute of Directors (SLID) Annual Members Meeting under the Chairmanship of Dinesh Weerakkody at the Cinnamon Grand, Samarasinghe who was Sri Lanka’s envoy to the US, said that the US accounts for 25% of exports and protecting it was of vital importance.

He said that due to successful negotiations and goodwill of the US, Sri Lanka was able to reduce the planned new tariff from a high of 44% to 33% and 10% progressively.

“This is not the end of the game. Negotiations are still taking place between Sri Lanka and the US to finalise the trade agreement,” he said at the SLID forum at which Chief Guest was Secretary to the Prime Minister G. Pradeep Saputhanthri and Guest of Honour was Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Republic of Indonesia to Sri Lanka and Diplomatic Corps in Sri Lanka Dean Dewi Gustina Tobing.

“We have finished 90% of the content of the agreement as I speak to you today, and of course, once we agree in principle to the content, we have to then embark on the domestic processes that are needed to give effect. Finally, to the legal effect, to come into action for signing it and then starting to implement the agreement,” he added.

“I have recommended very strongly to the Government that we need to conclude the agreement so that we can lock in the very favourable tariff rate that Sri Lanka has got up to now, and Government is committed to sorting out whatever differences that are there to give and take, and come to that agreement, so that there is some reliability, some assurance that can be given to domestic exporters that that market opportunity is available not only today but as we move forward,” said Samarasinghe who ended his stint at Sri Lanka’s Ambassador to the US recently.

“The bottom line on all these negotiations was that every country that finally agreed to sign the agreement had to give either complete duty-free access for American exports into those markets, or near complete duty-free access. Many countries who have signed the agreement have given complete access,” he added.

He also said that the US has been a friend of Sri Lanka over the years unconditionally and genuinely which must be recognised.

title: Govt. weighs fuel pricing options as global crude prices surge | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 15 September 2026 06:05
-     - 11

Energy Minister Anura Karunathilaka yesterday said the Government is set to review fuel prices at the end of this month as a sharp rise in international crude oil prices puts pressure on the country’s domestic pricing regime.

Speaking to the media, he said fuel was currently being sold locally at prices below international market levels, while private distributors had repeatedly warned that they could not sustain operations under the prevailing pricing conditions.

“The distributing companies have flagged a loss of around Rs. 140 and 160 per litre. The Government is therefore considering several options to address the widening gap between domestic prices and global costs, while seeking to protect consumers from a sharp increase,” he added.

Karunathilaka said one option was to provide concessions, similar to Government interventions in April and May that cushioned consumers from higher international prices. Another option under consideration is a price-band mechanism, under which fuel companies would be permitted to sell within a defined minimum and maximum range.

“We will consider all of this and make a decision. The interests of fuel consumers, as well as the grievances of private companies, will be taken into account,” he said.

The Minister stressed that the Government would seek to balance fuel affordability for consumers with the financial sustainability of fuel distribution.

He said the final decision would be based on an assessment of international oil market trends as well as conditions in the domestic market, with the next fuel price calculation due at the end of the month.

FitsAir has temporarily suspended its daily flights to Dubai.

The suspension was from 6 September and the budget carrier linked it to the evolving global situation and its impact across the Middle East.

"We currently expect to resume services by November 2026 subject to developments in the region," FitsAir added.

FitsAir began daily flights to Dubai in March 2023, having begun four times a week.

title: Global uncertainties placing increasing burden on businesses | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 15 September 2026 05:59
-     - 10

The second round of the Industry Index survey conducted by IFH KÖLN and Messe Frankfurt shows that, whilst the global business climate has remained largely unchanged overall compared with the first round and remains at a subdued level, the factors causing pressure have shifted significantly. 

In particular, global uncertainties, rising production and procurement costs, as well as tariffs and trade restrictions, are putting companies under increasing pressure.

The global industry index compiled by IFH KÖLN and Messe Frankfurt serves as an international sentiment barometer, highlighting developments in trade fair-related sectors at an early stage.

A total of 667 representatives from Industry and Trade and Service around the world took part in the second survey wave in June and July 2026. With an index score of 100.4, compared with 100.1 in the first survey wave, the global business climate remains virtually unchanged and subdued overall. The industry is slightly more confident than Trade and Service. There are also regional differences: Asia is 4.2 index points above the overall index and America 2.3 points above it, while Europe is 1.2 points below. 

IFH KÖLN Head of Strategic Insights and Analytics Dr. Ralf Deckers said: “The economy is currently less in recovery mode than under pressure to reposition itself. Sentiment is stabilising in some areas, but at the same time the pressures are shifting away from weak demand towards geopolitical uncertainty, rising costs, and trade barriers.” 

 

Costs and geopolitical crises move to centre stage

A comparison of the two survey rounds illustrates particularly clearly how the challenges facing businesses are shifting. In the manufacturing sector, 84% now cite global uncertainty caused by wars and conflicts as a key challenge – compared with 52% in the first survey round. At the same time, rising production costs are becoming significantly more important: the proportion citing this has risen from 51 to 66%. Global uncertainty is also rising significantly in the trade and services sector – from 46% to 63%. 

The second survey round coincided with a period of growing geopolitical tensions. The military conflicts in the Gulf region and the associated risks to key international trade and energy routes highlight just how closely intertwined geopolitical stability, global supply chains, and economic planning certainty are. At the same time, rising procurement costs are becoming a more significant factor, whilst consumer reluctance amongst private households is becoming less of a concern compared with the first survey wave. 

The second survey wave thus shows that companies are increasingly under pressure from both external factors that are difficult to influence and from rising costs.

Political pressures continue to increase

Tariffs and trade restrictions are continuing to put pressure on businesses. Regionally, businesses in America remain the hardest hit: 74% say they are severely or very severely affected. In Asia, the figure now stands at 66%, and in Europe at 42%. By way of comparison: in the first wave of the survey, the corresponding figures were 75% in America, 58% in Asia, and 33% in Europe. This means that the pressure is mounting, particularly in Asia and Europe. Despite this trend, companies do not feel significantly better prepared for changes to tariffs and import restrictions. A large proportion still consider themselves only partially prepared.

AI adoption faces structural hurdles

Another challenge is the use of artificial intelligence (AI). AI is currently used primarily for content creation and media-related applications. Its use is already somewhat more advanced in industry than in trade and services. 

According to the second wave of the survey, the biggest challenges in introducing AI lie primarily in a lack of expertise and in integration into existing systems. Budgetary issues, a lack of resources, as well as data protection and security risks also play a significant role.

Moderate outlook despite challenging conditions

Despite increased geopolitical and economic pressures, companies are not entirely pessimistic about the coming months. The industry sector, in particular, appears more confident about future developments than the trade and services sectors. The slight improvement in turnover also points to the first signs of recovery. Overall, however, expectations remain cautious. 

“Companies are increasingly adapting to the volatile environment, but there is still no sign of a broad-based upturn,” added Dr. Deckers. 

Messe Frankfurt Vice President – Consumer Goods Fairs Julia Uherek said: “Against this backdrop, businesses need clear direction, reliable networks, and new business contacts more than ever. International platforms such as the Frankfurt consumer goods fairs bring the right partners together for this purpose. We cannot eliminate volatility – but we can support companies in dealing with it more effectively.”

The launch was organised by the Ceylon Gem and Jewellery Traders Association (CGJTA).

The event was attended by the Chief Guest, Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Minister Sunil Handunnetti, who delivered the keynote address. 

He highlighted the importance of value addition, innovation and international collaboration in strengthening Sri Lanka’s gem and jewellery industry, as well as the significant opportunities for Sri Lanka–Thailand cooperation in gem cutting, processing, jewellery manufacturing, design, technology and international marketing.

The Minister further noted that Sri Lanka’s precious stones and centuries-old craftsmanship, together with Thailand’s globally recognised expertise in gemstone processing, jewellery manufacturing, design and international marketing, provided a strong foundation for deeper industry partnerships. He emphasised the potential to move beyond traditional trading relationships and strengthen cooperation through skills development, technology transfer, research and innovation.

Ambassador of Sri Lanka to Thailand, Wijayanthi Edirisinghe, participated in a panel discussion on “Strengthening Sri Lanka’s Gem and Jewellery Industry and Expanding Its Global Presence”, alongside National Gem and Jewellery Authority (NGJA) Chairman Dr. S. P. Chaminda, and other industry leaders.

Sri Lankan exports to Thailand more than doubled in 2025, reaching over $ 90 million from approximately $ 41.6 million in 2024, with precious and semi-precious stones accounting for almost 70% of Sri Lanka’s exports to Thailand.

“Gem Sri Lanka 2027”, scheduled to be held in Sri Lanka in January 2027, is expected to provide an important platform for international buyers, investors and industry stakeholders to explore Sri Lanka’s gem and jewellery sector and establish new business partnerships.

It will also look at the experience of businesses and international institutions operating across the region, providing perspectives on how companies assess markets, build supply chains and identify locations for investment. With supply chains and investment flows increasingly shaped by regional connectivity, the session will also consider the partnerships and strategies needed to position Sri Lanka as a more competitive participant in Asia’s growth networks, while creating opportunities for trade, investment, innovation and economic growth.

title: Hayleys Solar commissions 3MW Veyangoda Ground-Mounted Solar Project | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 15 September 2026 05:47
-     - 27

A commemorative plaque being presented to Ports and Civil Aviation Minister and Energy Minister Anura Karunathilake (right) by Managing Director Hasith Premathillake (centre) and Hayleys Fentons Deputy Managing Director – Energy Roshane Perera

Hayleys Solar marked a major milestone in its renewable energy journey with the opening of its 3MW Veyangoda Ground-Mounted Solar Project, with Energy Minister Anura Karunathilake gracing the occasion. 

The project marks the first of Hayleys Solar’s planned 300MW portfolio of ground-mounted solar power projects across Sri Lanka, further strengthening its commitment to expanding large-scale renewable energy solutions.

Hayleys Solar is part of Hayleys Fentons Ltd., under the Hayleys Group – Sri Lanka’s most diversified blue-chip conglomerate with a business legacy spanning nearly 150 years across 17 sectors. The Veyangoda project reflects the Group’s continued investment in expanding its renewable energy footprint in line with its long-standing commitment to sustainable innovation and nation-building.

Located adjacent to the Aththanagalla Oya, the project was designed to withstand challenging environmental conditions, including potential flooding during heavy rainfall. Following a detailed assessment using historical data from the Irrigation Department, Hayleys Solar implemented an elevated solar mounting structure with increased clearance and safety margins, together with elevated inverter supports and customised cable routing systems to enhance the project’s resilience.

Highlighting the importance of private sector participation in Sri Lanka’s energy transition, Energy Minister Anura Karunathilake said: “Building a secure and sustainable energy future for Sri Lanka requires us to harness the potential of renewable energy while encouraging greater participation from the private sector. Projects such as these demonstrate how investment, innovation and climate-resilient solutions can come together to support this national priority. We encourage more such initiatives that can strengthen our renewable energy capacity and contribute to a cleaner and more sustainable Sri Lanka.”

Hayleys Fentons Ltd., Managing Director Hasith Prematillake said: “The Veyangoda project demonstrates our commitment to developing renewable energy solutions that respond to the realities of our environment. By integrating climate-resilient engineering with innovative land utilisation, we have created a solar installation that not only withstands challenging site conditions but also delivers greater value from the available land.”

The 3 MW Hayleys Solar Veyangoda Ground-Mounted Solar Project, inaugurated as the first project under the 300 MW ground-mounted solar rollout

The project comprises 4,143.36 kWp of DC capacity and 3MW of AC capacity, featuring 640W bifacial solar panels, and is expected to generate approximately 6,351,770.88 kWh of clean electricity annually - enough to meet the annual electricity needs of around 2,700 average Sri Lankan households¹ while avoiding approximately 4,339.53 tonnes of CO2 emissions each year.

With an average clearance of approximately 2.7 metres above ground level, the elevated structure also enables productive use of the land beneath the solar panels. As part of an agrivoltaic initiative, the space will support the cultivation of vegetables such as Scotch bonnet pepper and brinjal, enabling agricultural production alongside renewable energy generation.

Hayleys Fentons Ltd., Deputy Managing Director – Energy Roshane Perera said: “Our Veyangoda project showcases how innovative solar designs can deliver multiple benefits from a single site. The elevated configuration enhances flood resilience while improving airflow beneath the panels and supporting greater utilisation of reflected sunlight through bifacial technology. The planned agrivoltaic initiative further demonstrates how renewable energy generation and agriculture can coexist productively.”

The Veyangoda project reinforces Hayleys Solar’s commitment to advancing resilient, sustainable and innovative renewable energy solutions while supporting Sri Lanka’s transition towards a cleaner energy future.

title: Pick a Book steps beyond reading to preserve the human edge in AI age | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 15 September 2026 04:00

By Shanika Sriyananda

Can AI bring the joy and imagination that a book gives? Can it provide the warmth of a conversation that brings soul-to-soul connection? Can it inspire a love of reading and, most importantly, can it give us the smell of a new book?

These questions were among those raised at the recently held Readers’ Summit 2026, organised by Pick a Book under the theme ‘Human edge begins with reading’, which brought writers, leading entrepreneurs, readers and publishers together.

Pick a Book Sri Lanka, a seven-year-old reading movement, is now moving beyond book clubs, seeking to build a national ecosystem of readers, authors, publishers and booksellers as artificial intelligence transforms how people access information.

When was the last time you had a real conversation — not an exchange on Instagram or Facebook, or even a voice message, but a conversation that began with an idea and went somewhere?

That was the question posed by Barista Coffee Lanka Director and CEO Dilupa Pathirana, at the Readers’ Summit in Colombo, as he explored the relationship between reading, knowledge and human connection.

“Because for a conversation, you need a topic,” Pathirana said, adding that the material for that conversation comes from what people have listened to, experienced and, ultimately, read.

In an age in which people are bombarded with information, his message gives greater meaning to the objective of the summit, which promotes the idea that reading matters not simply because books contain knowledge, but because they give people something to think about and talk about.

“We are having a conversation with somebody who lived 500 years ago,” Pathirana said, describing the extraordinary reach created by writing and books.

For him, writing represented one of humanity’s great leaps. Spoken communication allowed people to warn one another of danger or point out where food could be found. Writing went further, allowing one person to leave a thought for someone else to discover long after the writer was gone.

The question of what happens to reading when machines can increasingly do the reading for us was placed at the centre of the Pick a Book 2026 campaign.

Pathirana’s answer was to look back at what writing and reading have enabled humans to do: preserve thoughts, share knowledge across generations and engage in conversations with people who lived centuries before us.

Founded seven years ago as a network of book clubs, Pick a Book is now attempting to turn its community into a much larger reading ecosystem.

Pick a Book Founder Ragulan Tharmakulasingam believes the rise of artificial intelligence makes the proposition more urgent.

“We are living through a moment where machines can read everything and understand almost none of it, and where attention has become the scarcest thing any of us owns,” he said. “In that world, reading is no longer a pastime. It is the human edge.”

The movement has already moved beyond simply encouraging people to buy and read books. Members discuss and debate them, exchange them, donate them and gift them, turning reading from a solitary activity into a social one.

“Pick a Book is a platform of possibilities, where books open doors to knowledge, meaningful connections, and the lifelong journey of becoming your best self,” Ragulan said, adding that its next phase is considerably more ambitious.

The movement plans to establish specialised clubs aimed at different communities, including CEO, entrepreneurs’, fiction and mindfulness clubs. But the centrepiece of its 2027 roadmap is The Serendib Circle, a proposed ecosystem connecting book clubs, authors, publishers and booksellers.

The idea is to give individual clubs access to infrastructure, technology and networks that would be difficult to create independently, while allowing them to maintain their own identities.

“Most book clubs run on passion, but they can’t build a platform, a home, the technology or the connections on their own. That takes scale. So we’re opening ours. The things you couldn’t build alone but now shared,” Ragulan said.

The program will give authors direct access to engaged readers, publishers a network of reading communities and booksellers a channel to some of the country’s most active book buyers.

More importantly, it represents a change in scale for Pick a Book - from creating readers to connecting the institutions and communities that make a reading culture possible.

That idea fits closely with the movement’s philosophy. A book does not have to provide the final answer. It can instead create the question that leads to another book, another conversation or another way of seeing the world.

Pick a Book’s social initiative, Read and Rise, is also gaining momentum. Launched last year with the donation of 30,000 books to children and communities with limited access to reading material, the program is now moving towards developing sustained reading habits.

Weekly reading sessions are being conducted in underprivileged schools, shifting the focus from distributing books to developing regular readers.

“A book is a beginning, but a habit is what changes a life. This year we are moving from giving books to building readers, week after week, in the schools that need it most. Reading should never be a privilege,” Ragulan said.

The initiative is significant because while a book can be donated once, a reading habit can influence a child’s education, imagination and ability to engage with the world for years.

The summit reflected the movement’s increasingly broad reach, bringing together business leaders, authors, educators and literary figures.

Ragulan’s second novel, ‘The Last Cup of Tea’, was also launched at the summit, bringing a deeply personal dimension to an event focused on the value of reading.

The book explores motherhood, identity, loss and transformation, built around Ragulan’s idea that a woman is, in a sense, born twice - first as a woman and again when she becomes a mother.

He reflected on how families celebrate the birth of a child while rarely recognising that the same moment also marks the birth of a mother.

The final section of the book moves into fiction, with its family, characters and story shaped by personal experiences and emotions.

“The feeling behind it is not,” he said, explaining that although the story is fictional, some of the moments and emotions behind it came from experiences through which he had come to understand himself.

The book, he said, is not only about his own mother but about motherhood in a wider human context.

“The mother is part of my complete civilisation,” he said.

Alongside Pathirana, John Keells Group OCTAVE Chief Growth Officer  Rohan Jayaweera spoke on ‘Readers’ Advantage: Winning in the Age of AI’, while leadership educator Vidusha Nathavitharana spoke on the value of reading from his childhood and revealed the ‘Books that he would save from a fire’.

Moderated by corporate trainer Prassanna Pathmanathan, a panel featuring Gratiaen Prize-winning writer Dr. Ramya Jirasinghe, award-winning author and administrative officer Ciara Mandulee, and Sarasavi Bookshop Director Amendra Haputhanthri discussed how a simple thought can develop until it becomes a novel or a book.

The discussion brought together different stages of the publishing journey, from the creation of an idea and the writing process to the eventual relationship between books and their readers.

ESU International Public Speaking Competition 2026 Winner Omar Hazari also spoke at the summit about pages, chapters and books, and how small steps shape our lives. He also spoke about how he was inspired to read through his mother’s encouragement.

For Pick a Book, the next seven years could therefore be very different from the first seven. The movement is now asking individuals not only to pick up a book, but also to build the networks, habits and communities needed to make reading a national culture.

“Those are exactly the capacities that reading builds,” Ragulan said, referring to thinking, imagination and deeper human connection.

“For seven years, we asked people to pick a book, but now we are asking a nation to pick each other up -  one reader, one club, one story at a time.”

Sri Lanka and Thailand further strengthened bilateral cooperation in the field of labour with the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on Labour Cooperation and a Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) on the Employment of Sri Lankan Workers in Thailand yesterday in Bangkok.

The two instruments were signed by Foreign Affairs, Foreign Employment and Tourism Minister Vijitha Herath and Thai Labour Minister Julapun Amornvivat. The agreements follow sustained negotiations between the relevant authorities of the two countries and establish a structured and transparent framework for the recruitment and employment of Sri Lankan workers in Thailand, while promoting their rights, welfare, and protection.

The signing marks an important milestone in the expansion of safe, regular, and mutually beneficial labour mobility between Sri Lanka and Thailand. The Thai Cabinet has approved the recruitment of an initial 10,000 Sri Lankan workers through the established legal framework to address labour shortages in Thailand. The MoU provides a framework for cooperation in areas including labour policies and practices, labour market information, skills development, labour productivity, labour protection, and the prevention of illegal recruitment and human trafficking.

The MoA establishes the practical arrangements for the recruitment and employment of Sri Lankan workers in Thailand, including transparent recruitment procedures, employment contracts, legal protection, welfare, visas and work permits, as well as return and repatriation arrangements. 

Together, the two instruments provide a comprehensive framework to facilitate the orderly employment of Sri Lankan workers while safeguarding their rights and welfare.

Minister Herath appreciated the opportunity given by the Royal Thai Government for Sri Lankan workers to seek employment in Thailand, and emphasised the importance of ensuring their rights, welfare, and social security. He also highlighted the need to establish a Joint Working Group to monitor and review the implementation of the agreements. 

In this context, Minister Herath also sought Thailand’s consideration of expanding employment opportunities for Sri Lankan nationals, particularly the youth, in the IT and tourism sectors, which could provide new avenues for skilled employment and contribute to the development of Sri Lanka’s youth workforce.

Minister Julapun said that the Sri Lankan workers employed under this framework will enjoy equal rights and protection under Thai labour law, including legally mandated wages, benefits, and health care. Beyond worker recruitment and employment, the MoU also provides a foundation for broader labour cooperation to strengthen the workforce of both countries in line with future labour market and economic developments.

The Government of Sri Lanka views Thailand and the wider Southeast Asian region as important emerging destinations for Sri Lankan workers, as Sri Lanka continues to explore and diversify new labour markets for its nationals. The similarities in social and cultural characteristics between Sri Lanka and many Southeast Asian countries are expected to enable Sri Lankan workers to adapt more readily to their new working and living environments.

The establishment of structured employment opportunities in Thailand is therefore an important step towards diversifying Sri Lanka’s foreign employment destinations, expanding opportunities for skilled workers and professionals, particularly youth, and further strengthening the longstanding and multifaceted relations between Sri Lanka and Thailand.

title: IESL National Engineering Conference 2026 to bring engineering, policy and industry leaders together for Sri Lanka’s future | Daily FT

The Institution of Engineers, Sri Lanka, will hold the National Engineering Conference 2026 on 24 September 2026 from 3 p.m. at Cinnamon Grand Colombo. The conference will bring together policymakers, senior government officials, engineers, academics, industry leaders, investors and development partners to discuss practical solutions for several important national challenges.

NEC 2026 is designed as more than a professional conference. IESL will present four policy papers prepared by engineering professionals and invite the relevant authorities and stakeholders to consider practical actions for implementation. The four areas are engineering education, energy transition and power sector reforms, transport sector development and building fire safety.

The first area focuses on engineering, technology and technical education. Sri Lanka needs an education and professional development system that responds to national needs while maintaining internationally recognised standards. The proposed policy seeks clearer categories for Engineers, Engineering Technologists and Engineering Technicians, together with defined competencies, qualifications and career pathways. It also highlights the importance of accreditation, workforce planning and stronger links between education, industry and professional practice. A well-planned system can provide young people with clearer opportunities while ensuring that the country develops the skills needed for future growth.

The second area is energy transition and power sector reform. The report finds that the main challenge is now implementation rather than the absence of policy. Renewable energy development must be managed as part of an integrated power system. Expansion of solar and wind generation must be supported by stronger transmission and distribution networks, energy storage, forecasting, demand management and system control. The sector must also balance energy security, reliability, affordability, financial sustainability and environmental responsibility. The report calls for better planning, stronger institutions, improved procurement, transparent tariffs, investor confidence and measurable performance.

Transport is the third priority. The proposal is to establish an integrated multimodal people-centred public transport system that provides fast, affordable, reliable, and seamless connectivity between cities, townships, economic centres, and rural nodes. The proposal considers an integrated fare and ticketing system, with first- and last-mile connectivity embedded into a national digital platform. Expected national-level benefits include reduced travel time, manageable congestion, reduced fuel consumption, lower logistics costs, enhanced productivity and improved regional connectivity.    

The fourth area addresses building fire safety. Sri Lanka currently has fragmented responsibilities and no single national authority responsible for the continuous regulation of building fire safety. The proposed framework calls for a National Building Fire Safety Act and an independent National Fire Safety Authority. It also proposes regular inspections, certification, clear technical standards, professional review and effective enforcement. These measures are intended to protect lives and property and create consistent safety standards across the country.

Through NEC 2026, IESL aims to bring engineering knowledge closer to national decision-making. The value of the conference will ultimately depend on how effectively these proposals are reviewed, developed and implemented. By bringing government, professionals, academia and industry together, NEC 2026 provides an opportunity to turn sound engineering ideas into practical national action.
